 1                                             COMPLAINT
 2          Plaintiffs Twitch Interactive, Inc. (“Twitch”) and Amazon.com, Inc. (“Amazon” and
 3   collectively, “Plaintiffs”), by and through their undersigned attorneys, bring this Complaint against
 4   Defendant Kirill Konstantinovich Malofeyev (“Malofeyev” or “Defendant”) and allege:
 5                                      NATURE OF THE ACTION
 6          1.      Twitch and Amazon bring this action to seek the protection of the U.S. courts and
 7   enjoin Malofeyev from enforcing an invalid Russian judgment that he obtained in breach of
 8   contractual promises, and that, if enforced, would cause Twitch and Amazon irreparable harm.
 9          2.      Malofeyev is a Russian national that the U.S. government sanctioned due to his role
10   in a “worldwide sanctions evasion and malign influence network” led by his father, sanctioned
11   Russian oligarch Konstantin Malofeyev.1 Malofeyev began using Twitch to stream videos of
12   himself playing video games in 2013 and agreed to the Twitch Terms of Service (the “Terms of
13   Service”) and amendments thereto. He also entered into a Content License and Base Network
14   Agreement (the “Content License Agreement”) with Twitch to earn revenues from his content
15   (referred to as “monetization”).
16          3.      The contracts mandate that disputes must be resolved through arbitration (as to the
17   Terms of Service) or litigation (as to the Content License Agreement) in California and governed
18   by California law. Amazon was not a party to either agreement and did not provide Twitch
19   streaming or monetization services to Malofeyev.
20          4.      Malofeyev sued both Twitch and Amazon in the Arbitrazh Court of the City of
21   Moscow (the “Russian Arbitrazh Court”) in violation of his contractual obligations with Twitch.
22   Malofeyev asked the court to require Plaintiffs to provide services to him under the contracts.
23   Malofeyev filed these claims in the Russian Arbitrazh Court even though Twitch had no physical
24   presence in Russia and Malofeyev had no contractual relationship with Amazon. Despite these and
25   other clear procedural and substantive bars, the Russian Arbitrazh Court allowed the case to
26
     1
27    U.S. Dep’t Treasury, U.S. Treasury Designates Facilitators of Russian Sanctions Evasion, Press
     Release (Apr. 20, 2022), https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy0731.
28

 1   proceed under a Russian law that was passed as a countermeasure to sanctions and purports to give
 2   sanctioned parties special rights to sue their U.S. counterparties in Russia. In December 2022,
 3   Malofeyev obtained an unconscionable and oppressive judgment against Twitch and Amazon (the
 4   “Russian Judgment”) for specific performance and a compounding penalty (called an “astreinte”)
 5   under Russian law. The penalty was initially 100,000 Russian rubles per day and purports to double
 6   each week without limit. This penalty has already reached astronomical levels and continues to be
 7   more astronomical with each passing day. This penalty is unjustified on any measure and is wholly
 8   disproportionate to the less than $2,000 that Malofeyev accrued from monetization during the entire
 9   life of the account.
10          5.      Malofeyev now seeks to enforce the Russian Judgment in Turkey (the “Turkish
11   Enforcement Action”), and possibly elsewhere. In addition, Malofeyev will likely attempt to
12   prevent Amazon and Twitch from proceeding with this action by filing a lawsuit seeking injunctive
13   relief in Russia under the same Russian law (supra ¶ 4) that was passed to counter sanctions (an
14   “anti-suit injunction”). Twitch and Amazon therefore seek, inter alia, to enjoin Malofeyev from
15   pursuing the Turkish Enforcement Action, any other pending or future enforcement actions, or any
16   anti-suit injunction in Russia and compel arbitration of claims in California under the Terms of
17   Service.
18                                               PARTIES
19          6.      Twitch is incorporated in Delaware, with its principal place of business in San
20   Francisco, California. Twitch is a real-time live-streaming video service where community
21   members gather to watch, play, and chat about shared interests—predominantly video games, but
22   also sports, creative arts, current events, and others. Twitch users who share live content on
23   Twitch’s website and related services, software, and networks (the “Twitch Services”)—known as
24   “streamers”—pursue their interests to engage and entertain their viewers. People from around the
25   world who are fans of a particular video game, subject area, or streamer use Twitch to find, view,
26   and engage with the content that interests them.
27          7.      Amazon is a technology company incorporated in Delaware, with its principal place
28
       COMPLAINT                                         2
         Case 3:25-cv-01850         Document 1        Filed 02/20/25     Page 4 of 25




 1   of business in Seattle, Washington. Amazon is the parent company of Twitch.
 2          8.      Defendant Malofeyev was an individual user of the Twitch Services and could
 3   monetize, i.e., earn revenue from, his user-generated content displayed on his Twitch account, for
 4   example through advertising and subscription fees. Malofeyev is a person designated as a
 5   sanctioned party by the U.S. Department of Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (“OFAC”)
 6   on its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List and, on information and belief,
 7   resides in Russia.
 8                                            JURISDICTION
 9          9.      This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction over the claims set forth herein pursuant
10   to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(2). Defendant and Plaintiffs are completely diverse. Twitch is a Delaware
11   corporation with its principal place of business in California. Amazon is a Delaware corporation
12   with its principal place of business in Washington. On information and belief, Malofeyev is a
13   citizen of Russia, a foreign state. Further, the amount in controversy far exceeds $75,000, exclusive
14   of interest and costs, based on the compounding penalty that the Russian Judgment has imposed
15   jointly and severally on Twitch and Amazon and the damages Twitch and Amazon have suffered
16   from Malofeyev’s contractual breaches.
17          10.     This Court also has subject-matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to 9 U.S.C.
18   § 4 by virtue of Twitch and Malofeyev’s agreement to arbitrate all disputes under the Terms of
19   Service. The Terms of Service, as amended, provide in Section 15(d)(i) that any dispute arising
20   from the Terms of Service or Malofeyev’s use of the Twitch Services will be arbitrated in Santa
21   Clara County, California (the “Arbitration Agreement”). (Ex. A § 15(d)(i).)
22          11.     This Court also has subject-matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to the
23   United Nations Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (the
24   “New York Convention”), to which the Russian Federation and the United States are parties. An
25   arbitration agreement “arising out of a legal relationship, whether contractual or not, which is
26   considered as commercial, including a transaction, contract, or agreement described in section 2 of
27   this title, falls under the convention.” 9 U.S.C. § 202. United States district courts “shall have
28
       COMPLAINT                                          3
         Case 3:25-cv-01850         Document 1        Filed 02/20/25     Page 5 of 25




 1   original jurisdiction” over any action or proceeding “falling under the Convention” because it shall
 2   be “deemed to arise under the laws and treatises of the United States.” 9 U.S.C. § 203.
 3          12.     This Court is authorized to award the requested declaratory and injunctive relief
 4   under the Declaratory Judgment Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 2201-02. An “actual controversy” exists in the
 5   Northern District of California regarding Twitch and Amazon because the Russian Judgment
 6   compels Plaintiffs to take action in the United States.
 7          13.     This Court has personal jurisdiction over Malofeyev because he agreed to be subject
 8   to the jurisdiction of this Court. The Content License Agreement contains a governing law,
 9   jurisdiction, and venue clause that provides: “[t]he Parties hereby consent to the exclusive
10   jurisdiction and venue” of the “courts located within San Francisco County in the State of
11   California” and “hereby waive any jurisdictional or venue defenses otherwise available to them.”
12   (Ex. B § 9.3.) In addition, pursuant to the Terms of Service as amended, Malofeyev consented to
13   personal jurisdiction in the Northern District of California by agreeing to arbitrate all disputes
14   arising from the Terms of Service or his use of the Twitch Services in Santa Clara County,
15   California. (Ex. A § 15(d)(i).)
16          14.     Malofeyev also has sufficient minimum contacts with California and the United
17   States because Malofeyev seeks to cause Twitch and Amazon to take action within California and
18   the United States to comply with the Russian Judgment—specifically, to take actions to restore his
19   Twitch account, provide the Twitch Services and make a payment in accordance with the
20   compounding penalty imposed by the Russian Judgment.
21                                     DIVISIONAL ASSIGNMENT
22          15.     Venue is proper in the San Francisco Division because Malofeyev “consent[ed] to
23   the exclusive jurisdiction and venue” of the “courts located within San Francisco County in the
24   State of California” and waived “any jurisdictional or venue defenses” under the Content License
25   Agreement. (Ex. B § 9.3.) Venue also lies in this District and Division because Malofeyev
26   consented to venue in the Northern District of California under the Terms of Service as amended
27   and because, under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2), a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise
28

 1   to the claims, namely the suspension of his Twitch account, the Twitch Services and monetization
 2   services, occurred in San Francisco. (See Ex. A § 15(d)(i).)
 3                                      FACTUAL BACKGROUND
 4   A.     Malofeyev Creates a Twitch Account and Agrees to the Twitch Terms of Service.
 5          16.     On or about May 19, 2013, Malofeyev created a Twitch account using the name
 6   “likkrit” (the “Account”) and thereafter began streaming content on his channel showing himself
 7   playing video games.
 8          17.     When Malofeyev created the Account, he agreed to the Terms of Service. (Ex. C.)
 9   Amazon was not a party to the Terms of Service.
10          18.     The Terms of Service established that “Twitch, in its sole discretion, for any or no
11   reason, and without penalty, may terminate any account (or any part thereof) you may have with
12   Twitch or your use of the Twitch Service and remove and discard all or any part of your account,
13   User profile, and any Broadcaster Content, at any time.” (Ex. C § 11(1).) In return for agreeing to
14   the Terms of Service, Malofeyev was granted use of the Twitch Services, including “all related
15   services, software applications and networks that allow for the authorized streaming and
16   distribution of video content over the internet.” (Id. § 1.)
17          19.     The Terms of Service further provided that Malofeyev’s continued use of the Twitch
18   Services would constitute his binding agreement to any future amendments, modifications to, and
19   iterations of the Terms of Service. (Ex. C § 5.) The Terms of Service were amended at various
20   times between 2013 and April 2022, with the latest applicable amendments dated January 1, 2021.
21   (Ex. A.) Malofeyev agreed to these amendments through his continued use of the Twitch Services.
22          20.     The amended Terms of Service included the Arbitration Agreement, under which
23   Malofeyev agreed to arbitrate in California all disputes arising from the Terms of Service or his use
24   of the Twitch Services, such as disputes relating to the termination, suspension, or reinstatement of
25   those services. The Terms of Service, as amended, stated that:
26          You and Twitch agree to arbitrate any dispute arising from these Terms of Service
            or your use of the Twitch Services . . . . ARBITRATION PREVENTS YOU FROM
27          SUING IN COURT OR FROM HAVING A JURY TRIAL. . . . You and Twitch
28

             further agree . . . that any arbitration will occur in Santa Clara County, California;
 1           that arbitration will be conducted confidentially by a single arbitrator in accordance
 2           with the rules of JAMS . . . . Any dispute between the parties will be governed by
             this Agreement and the laws of the State of California and applicable United States
 3           law, without giving effect to any conflict of laws principles that may provide for the
             application of the law of another jurisdiction.
 4           (Ex. A § 15(d)(i).2)
 5           21.    Under the amended Terms of Service, Malofeyev also agreed that Twitch could
 6   block or terminate his account at any time: “To the fullest extent permitted by applicable law,
 7   Twitch reserves the right, without notice and in our sole discretion, to terminate your license to use
 8   the Twitch Services (including to post User Content) and to block or prevent your future access to
 9   and use of the Twitch Services, including where we reasonably consider that: (a) your use of the
10   Twitch Services violates these Terms of Service or applicable law . . . .” (Ex. A § 14.)
11           22.    The Twitch Community Guidelines (the “Community Guidelines”) are a set of
12   policies relating to user-generated content and behavior. In the amended Terms of Service,
13   Malofeyev agreed that he would “comply with these Terms of Service and Twitch’s Community
14   Guidelines.” (Ex. A § 9.) The Community Guidelines stated that “we at Twitch reserve the right
15   to suspend any account at any time for any conduct we determine to be inappropriate or harmful.”
16   (Ex. D at 2.) The Community Guidelines referred to the Twitch “About Suspensions” page, which
17   was hyperlinked in the Community Guidelines. The “About Suspensions” page stated: “If you are
18   indefinitely suspended, you will not be able to utilize Twitch monetization tools during your
19   suspension and existing recurring subscriptions to your channel will not renew.” (Ex. E at 2.)
20   B.      Malofeyev Enters into the Content License Agreement.
21           23.    On February 3, 2016, Malofeyev entered into the Content License Agreement with
22   Twitch to monetize his user-generated content on Twitch, i.e., the content he created, streamed,
23   and/or stored on his Account, through, for example, advertising and subscription fees. Amazon
24   was not a party to the Content License Agreement.
25           24.    The Content License Agreement contained a forum-selection clause at Section 9.3,
26

27   party “is a resident in any jurisdiction in which the [arbitration provision] is found to be
     unenforceable.” (Ex. A § 15(d)(ii).) This exception does not apply here.

 1   under which Malofeyev agreed that any “legal suit, action or proceeding arising out of or relating
 2   to this Agreement by a Party will be resolved by litigation in the courts located within San Francisco
 3   County in the State of California” (the “Forum-Selection Clause”). (Ex. B § 9.3.) The parties
 4   “consent[ed] to the exclusive jurisdiction and venue of such courts, and “waive[d] any jurisdictional
 5   or venue defenses otherwise available to them.” (Id.)
 6   C.       Malofeyev Is Sanctioned, and Twitch Suspends His Account Indefinitely.
 7            25.     After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the U.S. government
 8   imposed additional economic sanctions on Russian individuals and entities. On April 20, 2022,
 9   OFAC designated Malofeyev as a sanctioned party for his involvement “in attempts to evade
10   sanctions imposed by the United States and its international partners on Russia.”3 OFAC’s
11   designation of Malofeyev was a part of the U.S. government’s efforts to target a “worldwide
12   sanctions evasion and malign influence network” led by Defendant’s father.4
13            26.     Following OFAC’s designation, Twitch ceased doing business with Malofeyev. On
14   April 27, 2022, Twitch provided notice to Malofeyev that Twitch had suspended his Account and
15   restricted his access to the Twitch Services indefinitely due to U.S. sanctions (the “Account
16   Suspension”).
17            27.     After his Account was suspended, Malofeyev no longer had access to the Account
18   or monetization services.
19   D.       Malofeyev Sues Twitch and Amazon Jointly in Russia, Breaching His Agreement to
20            Resolve Disputes with Twitch in California.
21            28.     Following the Account Suspension, Malofeyev filed lawsuits in Russia against
22   Twitch and Amazon in or around June and October 2022, raising claims arising from the Terms of
23   Service and his use of the Twitch Services and arising out of or relating to the Content License
24   Agreement. These suits were in clear violation of his agreement to resolve all disputes relating to
25

 1   the Terms of Service, his use of the Twitch Services and the Content License Agreement in
 2   California. The suits also ignored that Amazon was not a party to either agreement.
 3          29.        Malofeyev filed the June 2022 suit in the Russian Arbitrazh Court, which dismissed
 4   it without prejudice.
 5          30.        Malofeyev filed the October 2022 suit in the Perovsky District Court of Moscow,
 6   which transferred the case back to the Russian Arbitrazh Court. Per a later ruling by the Russian
 7   Arbitrazh Court, infra ¶¶ 33-36, Malofeyev asserted, inter alia, that he entered into a contract with
 8   Twitch by agreeing to the Terms of Service and he began receiving monetization under the Content
 9   License Agreement. He requested that the Russian Arbitrazh Court “invalidate repudiation” of the
10   Content License Agreement and Terms of Service and order Twitch and Amazon to reinstate
11   services or pay an astreinte.
12          31.        On or about November 3, 2022, the Russian Arbitrazh Court issued an ex parte
13   ruling accepting the case for consideration and setting an in-person hearing on December 8, 2022.
14          32.        Twitch and Amazon received notice of the December 8, 2022 hearing only a few
15   days before it took place. This notice was inadequate, and Plaintiffs were not present or represented
16   at the hearing.
17          33.        The Russian Arbitrazh Court ruled on the merits of Malofeyev’s claims at the
18   December 8, 2022 hearing. The court applied Russian law, even though the Terms of Service and
19   the Content License Agreement are governed by California law. In particular, the court cited
20   Russian Law No. 127-FZ, which is specifically designated, per its title, to “Influence (Counter)
21   Unfriendly Actions of [the] USA and [O]ther [F]oreign [S]tates,” to find that U.S. sanctions are
22   “unfriendly U.S. actions threatening the territorial integrity of the Russian Federation and aimed at
23   its economic and political destabilization.” (Ex. F at 3.) The Russian Arbitrazh Court also
24   concluded that Article 248.1 of the Arbitrazh Procedural Code of the Russian Federation
25   established its jurisdiction over the dispute, because it involved a sanctioned party. Article 248.1
26

27

28
       COMPLAINT                                           8
          Case 3:25-cv-01850        Document 1        Filed 02/20/25       Page 10 of 25




 1   was enacted by Russia in June 2020 under Law No. 171-FZ5 to counter the impact of sanctions
 2   from “unfriendly foreign states,” including the U.S., and purports to grant the Russian arbitrazh
 3   courts “exclusive jurisdiction” over disputes involving Russian individuals sanctioned by foreign
 4   states.6 (Ex. G at 1.) These Russian laws deliberately favor Russian parties and have been abused
 5   to obtain onerous and unconscionable penalties against U.S. entities in violation of binding
 6   contractual agreements. The court asserted its jurisdiction even though Article 248.1 expressly
 7   carves out circumstances where jurisdiction is “otherwise provided by . . . agreement of the parties,”
 8   such as in a forum-selection clause or arbitration agreement. (Id. at 1.)
 9           34.     The Russian Arbitrazh Court treated Amazon as a party to Malofeyev’s agreements
10   with Twitch based on Malofeyev’s claims. The court concluded that Twitch is “100% . . . owned
11   by Amazone.com Inc. [sic], which defines Twitch Interactive Inc.’s [sic] user policy.” (Ex. F at 2.)
12   Without any other factual basis, the Russian Arbitrazh Court held that Twitch and Amazon
13   “collectively provide platform services to the users.” (Id. at 5.)
14           35.     The Russian Arbitrazh Court found in favor of Malofeyev’s claim that Twitch and
15   Amazon had violated his rights by suspending the Account and monetization services. The court
16   found that Twitch and Amazon engaged in an “unlawful unilateral refusal to provide the services”
17   under Russian law and ordered both Twitch and Amazon to restore Malofeyev’s Account and
18   provide Malofeyev with the Twitch Services and monetization under the applicable agreements.
19   (Ex. F at 2.)
20           36.     As requested by Malofeyev, the Russian Arbitrazh Court imposed a compounding
21   penalty on Twitch and Amazon if they did not comply with the court’s order for specific

 1   performance, commencing in the amount of 100,000 Russian rubles for each day of non-
 2   performance and doubling each week without limit, reaching astronomical levels. (Ex. F at 1, 5,
 3   6.) Because this penalty doubles each week, it purportedly is now larger than all the money in the
 4   world. The astreinte is unjustified on any measure and is wholly disproportionate to the less-than-
 5   $2,000 in revenue generated by Malofeyev’s Account while active.
 6   E.      Malofeyev Seeks to Enforce the Russian Judgment Outside of Russia Against Twitch
 7           and Amazon.
 8           37.    On November 3, 2023, Malofeyev filed the Turkish Enforcement Action to
 9   recognize and enforce the Russian Judgment and the astreinte penalty against Twitch and Amazon
10   before the Istanbul 19th Commercial Court of First Instance in Turkey (the “Turkish Commercial
11   Court”). (Ex. H.)
12           38.    Malofeyev served the Turkish Enforcement Action on a subsidiary of Amazon,
13   Amazon Turkey Perakende Hizmetleri Şirketi (“Amazon Turkey”), which is based in Turkey.
14   Malofeyev claimed that Amazon Turkey was a “representative” of Twitch and Amazon for the
15   purpose of service. (Ex. H at 1.)
16           39.    The Turkish Commercial Court held that Twitch and Amazon received service of
17   the Turkish Enforcement Action by virtue of service on Amazon Turkey.
18           40.    At the time of this filing, the Turkish Enforcement Action is pending. The first
19   hearing on the merits is scheduled to take place on February 27, 2025. All hearings to date have
20   been on procedural matters.
21   F.      Twitch and Amazon Will Be Irreparably Harmed by Malofeyev’s Enforcement
22           Efforts.
23           41.    Plaintiffs will face irreparable harm from Malofeyev’s enforcement attempts for the
24   following reasons.
25           42.    First, Plaintiffs have been denied any remedy for Malofeyev’s breach of the
26   Arbitration Agreement in the Terms of Service and Forum Selection Clause in the Content License
27   Agreement. Plaintiffs have been deprived of legal certainty provided by those agreements and
28
          COMPLAINT                                     10
         Case 3:25-cv-01850         Document 1        Filed 02/20/25      Page 12 of 25




 1   subjected to the Russian courts’ application of Russian laws specifically designed to undermine
 2   U.S. sanctions. Plaintiffs now must defend themselves against Malofeyev’s efforts to enforce a
 3   court order that would compel Plaintiffs to provide services to a sanctioned party and pay a
 4   compounding penalty in violation of U.S. law.
 5          43.     Second, Amazon has further been deprived of legal certainty by Malofeyev’s
 6   assertion of contract claims against Amazon. Amazon was named as a defendant in the Russian
 7   Judgment even though it had no contractual relationship with Malofeyev, is a separate legal entity
 8   from Twitch, and provided no services to Malofeyev. The Russian court nevertheless held Amazon
 9   and Twitch jointly liable without any basis in law or fact. Amazon will suffer irreparable harm
10   from this loss of legal certainty as a result of Malofeyev’s baseless claims.
11          44.     Finally, Malofeyev seeks to enforce the Russian Judgment in his favor against
12   Plaintiffs in Turkey and, on information and belief, in other jurisdictions. These enforcement
13   attempts are a direct attempt to force Plaintiffs to provide services to a party against their will and
14   pay a monetary penalty to a sanctioned party in violation of U.S. law. This causes Plaintiffs further
15   harm due to their need to defend against this action and the risk that they may be compelled to do
16   business with Malofeyev or pay a penalty and risk violating U.S. law.
17          45.     Absent an order from this Court enjoining Malofeyev’s efforts to enforce the
18   Russian Judgment, compelling arbitration as to the Terms of Service, and declaring that Malofeyev
19   must resolve all disputes arising from the Terms of Service or his use of the Twitch Services and
20   arising out of or relating to the Content License Agreement in California as he agreed to do,
21   Plaintiffs will continue to face the harms arising from his breach of contract.
22          46.     Plaintiffs consequently bring this action for breach of contract, declaratory and
23   injunctive relief, and to compel arbitration to stop Malofeyev’s improper conduct.
24                            FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION (AS TO TWITCH)
